title: The Chocolate Bar That Invented the Microwave

beats.say: Nineteen forty five. An engineer is standing next to a radar machine. Then he notices something strange. The chocolate bar in his pocket has melted.
That melted chocolate led to something in almost every kitchen. So how does a box with no fire cook your food?
The engineer was Percy Spencer. He left school at twelve to work in a mill, and taught himself science from books.
During the war, he built magnetrons. That's the part of a radar that sends out invisible waves to spot enemy planes.
After the chocolate, he got curious. He held some corn kernels near the machine. They popped into popcorn.
His company patented the idea. Their first oven, in nineteen forty seven, was taller than a person, and ended up in restaurants and on ships.
So what's the trick? Those invisible waves are like radio waves, only much shorter. We call them microwaves.
Food is full of water. And each tiny water molecule has a plus end and a minus end.
The waves keep flipping those ends back and forth, billions of times every second. All that jiggling makes heat.
Here's a surprise. A microwave doesn't cook from the inside out. The waves only reach a few centimetres in. The rest heats up from the outside, like normal.
Remember the chocolate? Try this with a grown-up. Take out the turntable, and heat a chocolate bar for about twenty seconds.
It melts in spots, where the waves are strongest. Measure the gap between them, do one simple sum, and you get the speed of light.
Today, in the US, ninety six in every hundred homes have a microwave. It all started with one melted chocolate bar. What would you have tested first?
